etymologies.etymologyHTML: First attested from 1603, from Middle French enthousiasme, from Late Latin enthusiasmus, from Ancient Greek ἐνθουσιασμός (enthousiasmós), from ἐν (en, “in”) + θεός (theós, “god”) + οὐσία (ousía, “essence”).

definitions.definition: Intensity of feeling; excited interest or eagerness.
Something in which one is keenly interested.

quote.citation: 1968, Central States Archaeological Journal, volumes 15-16, page 154:
quote.text: My main enthusiasm is attending and seeing the progress and interest of collectors, to meet old friends, and hopefully to make new friends.

quote.citation: 2012, Nicholas Joll, Philosophy and The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, page 23:
quote.text: Other Adamsian enthusiasms included: fast cars; restaurants; Bach, the Beatles, Pink Floyd and Dire Straits;  […]

definitions.definition: (obsolete or historical) Possession by a god; divine inspiration or frenzy.

quote.citation: 1946, Bertrand Russell, chapter 1, in History of Western Philosophy:
quote.text: The intoxication that they sought was that of ‘enthusiasm’, of union with the god.
